text:
This first laboratory connects the crystallographic language used in the course with an actual structure file. Before the session, review the ideas of unit cell, fractional coordinates, asymmetric unit, symmetry-equivalent positions and space group.
You are not expected to write Python code. The notebooks provide the code needed to inspect the structure. Your task is to understand what the calculation is doing and to interpret the crystallographic information that it returns.

title: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure
text:
A crystal structure is often first encountered as a picture: coloured spheres, polyhedra, chains, layers or frameworks. The picture is useful, but it is not the structure itself. A crystallographic model is a compact mathematical description of a periodic arrangement. In this laboratory we will start from that description and reconstruct the structure step by step.
The practical question is simple:
This is the first computational activity because it establishes a workflow that will return throughout the course: a structural model is read from data, analysed, visualized, checked against symmetry, and eventually used as the starting point for calculations of energy and physical properties.
crumbs: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure

title: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure
section: The CIF as a crystallographic description
text:
The CIF as a crystallographic description
The Crystallographic Information File (CIF) is a structured text format. For the present exercise, the most important information is the unit cell, the space group, the atomic sites, their fractional coordinates and their occupancies.
The fractional coordinate \((x,y,z)\) does not give a distance in ångström. Instead, it gives a position relative to the three direct-lattice vectors \(\mathbf{a}\), \(\mathbf{b}\), and \(\mathbf{c}\):
\[
\mathbf{r} = x\mathbf{a} + y\mathbf{b} + z\mathbf{c}.
\]
This is why the same fractional coordinates can describe geometrically different Cartesian positions when the cell parameters change.
A CIF normally does not need to list every atom that appears in a conventional unit cell. It can store only the crystallographically independent sites. The remaining sites follow from the symmetry of the space group.
crumbs: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure

title: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure
text:
Asymmetric unit and unit cell
The asymmetric unit is the smallest part of the structure from which the contents of the unit cell can be generated by applying the appropriate space-group operations. The unit cell, in turn, generates the infinite periodic crystal by translation.
This distinction is easy to lose when looking only at a structure drawing. MgO provides a particularly clean example. Only one Mg site and one O site are needed in its crystallographic description, but applying the symmetry and centring operations generates the complete contents of the conventional cubic cell.
In the notebook we therefore inspect the structure twice: first as the list of sites written in the CIF, and then as the symmetry-expanded unit cell. The difference between these lists is itself part of the crystallographic information.
crumbs: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure

title: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure
text:
Two complementary symmetry tools
We use Gemmi and spglib for different reasons.
Gemmi is used to read the CIF as a crystallographic document. It understands the unit cell, space-group symbols, symmetry operations and atomic sites. In other words, it can tell us what crystallographic information the file claims to contain.
spglib approaches the problem from another direction. We give it lattice vectors, atomic coordinates and atomic species. It then searches numerically for operations that map the structure onto itself. This requires a tolerance, because coordinates in real structure files are finite-precision numbers and experimental structures are never mathematical abstractions with infinitely exact coordinates.
The comparison is useful:
\[
\text{symmetry stated in the CIF}
\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{symmetry implied by the numerical structure}.
\]
Agreement is a consistency check. Disagreement is not something to hide by changing parameters until the desired answer appears. It is a result that must be understood: the structure may be distorted, the tolerance may be inappropriate, the CIF may use a non-standard setting, or the structural model may contain disorder or partial occupancies.
For this first exercise we use ordered structures with full occupancies so that the symmetry analysis remains unambiguous.
crumbs: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure

title: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure
text:
Symmetry operations in coordinate form
A space-group operation can be written as a transformation of fractional coordinates. The identity is
\[
(x,y,z)\rightarrow(x,y,z),
\]
whereas an operation written, for example, as
-y,x,z
maps
\[
(x,y,z)\rightarrow(-y,x,z).
\]
Translations may appear as fractional additions such as \(1/2\). Rather than printing every operation of a high-symmetry space group without context, the notebook first shows a compact set of Hall-derived operations and the lattice centring translations, and then lets you inspect part of the full operation list.
The software can describe the matrix and translational parts of an operation, but interpreting an operation geometrically remains a crystallographic task. In particular, the presence of a translational component is what distinguishes operations such as screw axes and glide planes from their purely point-symmetry counterparts.
crumbs: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure

title: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure
text:
Wyckoff positions
The atoms of a crystal can also be organized into Wyckoff positions. A Wyckoff position identifies an orbit of symmetrically equivalent points in a given space group.
Three pieces of information are especially useful:

the multiplicity, which gives the number of equivalent sites in the conventional unit cell;
the Wyckoff letter, which distinguishes inequivalent orbits;
the site symmetry, which describes the subgroup of operations that leaves a particular site invariant.

A multiplicity is therefore not the number of independent atoms that had to be entered in the CIF. Quite the opposite: several atoms in the conventional cell may all be generated from one crystallographically independent site.
crumbs: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure

title: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure
text:
Visualization is inspection, not proof
The notebooks use py3Dmol to display the CIF interactively. You can rotate the structure, zoom, draw the unit-cell box and replicate the cell to make periodicity easier to see.
The default representation uses spheres without automatically inferred bonds. This choice is deliberate. A line drawn between two atoms by a visualization program is based on a graphical or distance criterion; it is not itself a crystallographic observable and should not silently determine how we interpret bonding in a mineral.
The viewer is therefore an aid to scientific inspection. The quantitative description still comes from the crystallographic data and symmetry analysis.
crumbs: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure

title: Laboratory 1 — From CIF to crystal structure
text:
Laboratory workflow
The activity has two parts.
First, we work together on MgO (periclase):
01-guided-mgo.ipynb
MgO is useful because the rocksalt structure is simple enough that the relationship between asymmetric unit, face-centred cell, symmetry and Wyckoff multiplicity remains visible.
You will then receive a second CIF and repeat the same reasoning independently in:
02-assigned-structure.ipynb
Place the assigned CIF directly inside:
work/lab01/
and change only the filename requested in the notebook.
The questions are intentionally short. They ask you to interpret the structure, not to reproduce Python code.

title: Save, sync and stop

Saving a notebook and saving your work to GitHub are not the same operation.
This distinction is important.
Your GitHub repository is the safety copy that should survive beyond the lifetime of an individual Codespace.

title: Save, sync and stop
text:
Save your files
Save notebooks and other edited files normally with File → Save or Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on macOS).
A saved file is safe when a Codespace is merely stopped and restarted, but it has not yet been transferred to your GitHub repository.

title: Save, sync and stop
text:
Commit your work
Open Source Control using the branch-shaped icon in the left activity bar.
You will see the files that have changed.

Stage the relevant files using the + button.
Enter a short but meaningful commit message, for example:
Complete Lab 1 symmetry analysis
Select Commit.

For routine laboratory work it is acceptable to stage all files that belong to the current activity.






WarningIf you see “Publish Branch”



Your personal workspace should already be connected to a GitHub repository.
If Source Control asks you to Publish Branch instead of allowing you to synchronize normally, you may have opened a Codespace directly from the template rather than from your personal repository. Stop and ask the instructor before continuing.

title: Save, sync and stop
text:
Synchronize with GitHub
After committing, select Sync Changes.
If GitHub asks you to confirm the synchronization, accept the operation.
Then open your repository on GitHub in a normal browser tab and verify that your latest notebook or file is visible there.
This simple check is especially useful during the first laboratory.

title: Working in Codespaces
text: A GitHub Codespace is a remote Linux computer that you control through a browser-based Visual Studio Code interface. The interface contains many tools, but only a small subset is needed for this course.

title: Working in Codespaces
section: The four areas you will use
text:
The four areas you will use
Explorer
The file icon in the left activity bar. Use it to open notebooks and files and to navigate between course/ and work/.
Notebook editor
Opening an .ipynb file displays a Jupyter notebook. Run cells with the triangular Run button or with Shift+Enter. If you are asked to select a kernel, choose the Python environment provided by the Codespace.
Terminal
Open it with Terminal → New Terminal. Course commands such as update-course and start-lab are run here.
Source Control
The branch-shaped icon in the left activity bar. Use it to commit your work and synchronize it with GitHub.

title: Working in Codespaces
text:
Reopening your existing Codespace
After the first session, do not create a new Codespace every time.
You can reopen the existing one from either:

your personal workspace repository → Code → Codespaces; or
https://github.com/codespaces.

Starting an existing stopped Codespace is normally much faster than creating a new one.

title: How the laboratory works
text:
The computational laboratory uses a browser-based working environment so that all students can use the same scientific software without installing and configuring Python packages locally.
The working environment has three separate components.
The course website and your workspace are deliberately separate. You should not duplicate this website repository. Instead, you will create your own private repository from the dedicated Mineral Science workspace template.

title: How the laboratory works
text:
Your personal workspace
Your workspace repository contains two directories with very different roles:
course/
work/
course/ contains material distributed by the teacher. It may be updated during the course.
work/ contains your work: notebooks, answers, uploaded data, figures and processed results.






ImportantOne rule prevents most problems



Do not edit files directly inside course/. Work inside work/.


When a new laboratory is released, the usual workflow is:
update-course
      ↓
start-lab NN
      ↓
work/labNN/
      ↓
save → commit → sync
      ↓
stop Codespace
You do not need to understand Git internals to use this workflow. The necessary operations are introduced in the following pages.
